# Burr Grinder Alignment

## Overview

My espresso grinder uses flat steel burrs, and for two years the shots were inconsistent: one day balanced, the next gushing and sour. I blamed the beans until I realised the two burrs were not parallel. When the gap between the rings varies across the face, the grind has two distributions at once, fine on one side and coarse on the other. Aligning the burrs is the fix, and it is the single biggest upgrade I have made to the setup.

## Method

Start with the dry-erase marker test. Colour the flat face of the rotating burr with a marker, reassemble, and turn the motor by hand with the burrs set so they just touch. The marker rubs off wherever the metal meets, so the bare patches show the high spots and the untouched ink shows where the gap is wide.

To correct a tilt I use thin foil shims. The ones I keep are 0.05 mm and I stack them under the burr carrier until the contact pattern is even. A feeler gauge checks the gap at three points around the ring; I shim the low side and re-test. Small steps work best: add one shim, run the marker test again, and read the pattern before adding another.

## Troubleshooting

If the pattern is even but one section stays inked, the carrier may be warped or a screw is over-torqued. Loosen all three, seat the carrier gently and tighten in a cross pattern. Ghost burr contact is the other trap: the burrs touch when turned by hand, but the motor load makes them rub at speed and leaves a faint ring. That means you are sitting right at true zero, so back off a few microns.

The target is alignment under 10 microns across the full face. I confirm it with the gauge, check it with the marker, and only then dial in a shot. After any rebuild I re-check, because dropping the carrier or swapping burrs rarely leaves the old setting intact.
